newsitem.title: USA: Hillary Clinton stumps Ohio for expanded work leave.
newsitem.headline: Hillary Clinton stumps Ohio for expanded work leave.

text.p: First lady Hillary Rodham Clinton said Wednesday President Clinton favours expanding a federal law to allow parents time off from work to attend to family matters.
On a campaign trip to Ohio, she also said the president was right in signing a new welfare law and called upon employers to give welfare recipients jobs and guidance.

The Family and Medical Leave Act now enables workers to take up to 12 unpaid weeks' leave for family medical reasons. Clinton would like to expand it give workers some hours off to attend teacher conferences or take children or elderly parents to doctor appointments.

"The president has proposed that he would like to see Family and Medical Leave extended to include 24 hours during a year that would be available to employees to do the kinds of tasks that we want family members to do for each other," she told a mainly supportive audience at an Ohio hospital.
She toured a birthing centre at Lakewood Hospital in a Cleveland suburb and spoke as part of a panel there on medical care for new mothers and babies.
Mrs. Clinton praised Congress for the bipartisan effort that led to passage Tuesday of legislation assuring at least a two-day hospital stay for new mothers.

"I think with (this and other bipartisan efforts related to health care), we are beginning to see -- I hope -- more of a consensus that there are problems that need to be dealt with in a sensible manner and not be politicized," she said.
The president is expected to sign the measure as a counter to health insurers that have limited some hospital stays for new mothers to 24 hours.

Outside the hospital, a mostly friendly crowd of 50 or so watched Mrs. Clinton's car depart. However, one sign read, "FBI files -- who will pardon you?", a reference to a White House scandal in which a staffer allegedly compiled files on Republicans. Republicans have suggested the first lady was behind the action.

In answer to a question at her presentation, Mrs. Clinton said she believes her husband did the right thing in signing welfare reform into law. The bill continues government-paid medical coverage and nutrition assistance and, for people who go to work, increases child care assistance, she said.
"What we have to do, though, is take what used to be the welfare check and use it to subsidise employment in both the private and the public sector as the president has proposed," she said.
